newsitem.title: USA: European companies agree to $25 million U.S. fine.
newsitem.headline: European companies agree to $25 million U.S. fine.

text.p: Two European chemical companies agreed Wednesday to plead guilty of fixing the price of an important food additive and pay $25 million in criminal fines, the Justice Department announced.

Hoffmann-La Roche of Switzerland agreed to pay $14 million and Jungbunzlauer International AG, a subsidiary of the company of the same name in Austria, agreed to pay $11 million in the single-count felony.
They admitted they took part in an international criminal conspiracy to fix prices and allocate sales for the worldwide, $1.2 billion-a-year citric acid market.
The cartel raised the prices of citric acid, which is used in soft drinks, nearly all processed foods, detergents, textiles, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.

"The department will continue to seek out and prosecute all international conspiracies that increase prices for consumers and unfairly impede free and open competition in our markets," said Joel Klein, acting assistant attorney general of the antitrust division.

The Justice Department said that Udo Haas, former managing director of SA Citrique Belge NV, which produces citric acid for Hoffmann-La Roche, and Rainer Bichlbauer, chairman and president of Jungbunzlauer, agreed to plead guilty to the felonies and each pay a $150,000 fine.
The criminal charges were filed in federal court in San Francisco. A judge must approve the guilty pleas.
Several others in the cartel already have pleaded guilty, bringing the total in fines levied to $195 million.
Those fines included $50 million, which the Haarman & Reimer subsidiary of Bayer Co. agreed to in January, and $100 million which Decatur, Ill.-based Archer Daniels Midland Co. agreed to in October.

"With our new global economy, the antitrust division's top priority in criminal enforcement is to investigate and prosecute international cartels that hurt American consumers," said Gary Spratling, deputy assistant attorney geneeral for criminal enforcement in the antitrust division.

In an earlier civil case, Haarman & Reimer, Archer Daniels Midland, Hoffman-La Roche and Jungbunzlauer agreed to settle a price-fixing lawsuit brought by food procesors in California by paying them $94 million.
A fifth defendant, Cargill Inc., did not join the settlement, which was announced in December, 1996.
